overview: Trinidad and Tobago have distinct island histories, brought together in one country. Their everyday creativity includes stone tools, skilfully tuned steel, cooking traditions and community teaching. Each example below identifies its place and period.

periods.title: First Peoples’ long histories
periods.summary: Banwari Trace preserves evidence of settlement around 5000 BCE. This broad opening spans many communities and later changes; it is not the lifetime of one culture. First Peoples’ communities continue today.

periods.title: Spanish colonial Trinidad
periods.summary: Spanish colonial government developed in Trinidad from 1592. Tobago followed a separate history, including Dutch and French conflict in the seventeenth century.

periods.title: British capture and plantation slavery
periods.summary: Britain captured Trinidad from Spain in 1797; formal cession followed in 1802. Plantation production continued to rely on enslaved labour.

periods.title: Abolition followed by compulsory apprenticeship
periods.summary: The abolition law took effect in 1834, but many formerly enslaved people remained bound to compulsory apprenticeship until 1838.

periods.title: After full emancipation
periods.summary: Full emancipation came in 1838. Many freed people pursued livelihoods away from plantation control, while planters sought other sources of labour.

periods.title: Indian indentured migration
periods.summary: The first indentured workers from India reached Trinidad in 1845. Migration under this system continued to 1917, beyond the end of this selected phase.

periods.title: Trinidad and Tobago linked under British rule
periods.summary: An 1889 proclamation joined the islands under British administration. The union was a colonial change, separate from later independence.

periods.title: An independent constitutional monarchy
periods.summary: Trinidad and Tobago became independent on August 31, 1962, retaining the monarch as head of state, represented by a governor-general.

periods.title: The Republic of Trinidad and Tobago
periods.summary: The country became a republic on August 1, 1976, with a president as head of state.

sections.title: Discoveries: tools and a kitchen under the sea

items.text: At Banwari Trace in southern Trinidad, a settlement dating to around 5000 BCE, archaeologists found stone pestles, grinders, an axe and cutting flakes. Layers of discarded shells also survive. The tools and refuse reveal practical work and food gathering. A midden, archaeologists’ name for accumulated rubbish, can preserve an excellent record of everyday life, though it is nobody’s idea of a tidy kitchen.

At wreck site TRB-5 in Tobago’s Rockley Bay, a 2014 excavation recovered bricks still joined with mortar, copper sheet and wood fragments. Researchers interpreted these as possible remains of a ship’s galley, or kitchen. The finds date broadly to the seventeenth century; association with the 1677 battle is supported, but the vessel’s exact identity remained uncertain in the report.

The same test trench yielded four forks and five spoons. These small objects bring eating aboard ship into view alongside the cannon. They show that studying a wreck can recover traces of meals as well as battles. The report does not identify the diners, their food on a particular day, or whether everyone aboard had similar utensils.

NALIS’s account of Indian heritage in Trinidad names a belna, a rolling pin; a chauki, a board for working dough; and a sil and lorha, stones used for grinding. Such equipment accompanied cooking knowledge reshaped in Caribbean homes. Familiar foods involve practiced movements and specialised tools. The kitchen has its own vocabulary, and learning a word can also mean learning a skill.

Chinese shopkeepers became part of village life in Trinidad. NALIS describes a credit arrangement called trusting: customers could take groceries and pay later, while the shopkeeper recorded purchases and repayments in a copy book. A small notebook connected household needs with a local business. This is a documented practice, rather than a claim that every shop offered identical terms.

Trinidad’s immigration registers can record a person’s village in India, relatives, ship and assigned estate. These documents help descendants piece together family histories across oceans. Archivist Helena Leonce also describes missing records and arrivals through other Caribbean colonies. A gap in one register is a research problem, not evidence that a family has no history.

At Christmas, parang musicians visit homes with instruments such as the cuatro, guitar and maracas, while hosts offer food and drink. NALIS recalls nighttime visits that sometimes woke relatives and friends. It gives the idea of an alarm clock a much more musical interpretation. The account describes a particular festive tradition, not a rule followed by every household.

Steelpan developed through experimentation in Trinidad during the 1930s and 1940s. Makers shaped metal containers and tuned parts of the playing surface to different pitches. Earlier tamboo-bamboo groups made percussion music with cut bamboo tubes. The new instrument grew through many people’s work; accounts disagree about assigning its invention to a single person.

A steelband’s engine room is its percussion section, which helps keep the music moving together. NALIS lists bottle and spoon, maracas and assorted iron among its instruments. Here the engine runs on rhythm. The phrase is a useful reminder that a musical ensemble depends on timing and coordination as well as the performers carrying the tune.

In January 2023, Trinidad’s Santa Rosa First Peoples Community helped present the Caribbean Ties exhibition. Community members added baskets, hammocks, ceremonial clothing, photographs and foods including cassava. An ajoupa, a tapia hut, housed the exhibition. People shared their own knowledge and heritage in a community setting, showing that Indigenous history includes living voices as well as excavated objects.

Tobago’s Moriah Ole Time Wedding, documented in July 2017, recreated an older wedding celebration at the village’s Moravian church. A procession then carried the celebration through Moriah with participants and onlookers. It was a heritage performance, using humour and participation to share memories of social life. The staged ceremony should not be mistaken for a record of one historical couple’s marriage.

sections.title: Learning by doing, and political change

items.text: In a 2015 project concluding at Speyside Secondary School in Tobago, students built solar ovens from boxes, reflective material, insulation and clear plastic wrap. They tested the ovens with bread dough. The winning design baked its loaf all the way through. The exercise turned energy science into something visible and practical, with a result rather easier to inspect than an invisible sunbeam.

Independence and becoming a republic happened in different years. In 1962, Trinidad and Tobago became independent while retaining the monarch as head of state. In 1976, a president replaced that role. The distinction helps explain how a country can govern itself while still sharing a monarch with other countries.

ending.text: British colonial rule ended at independence in 1962; republican status followed in 1976. Trinidad and Tobago continues as a country. Its communities keep creating and sharing traditions, including First Peoples’ knowledge, music and food.
